result.summary: The hymn announces Hermes, born to Maia and Zeus in a cave on Cyllene. On the day of his birth he invents the lyre from a tortoise, then steals Apollo's cattle from Pieria, disguises their tracks, and drives them to the Alpheus, where he invents fire.

scenes.title: Birth of Hermes
scenes.summary: The Muse is asked to sing of Hermes, whom Maia bore to Zeus in secret in a cave. He is born a cunning thief who steals Apollo's cattle on his first day.
scenes.stakes: Zeus and Maia must keep their union hidden from Hera and the other gods.

scenes.title: Hermes invents the lyre
scenes.summary: Hermes finds a tortoise at the cave door, greets it, kills it and makes a seven-stringed lyre from the shell. He sings of his own begetting, then hides the lyre and sets out to steal meat.

scenes.title: Theft of the cattle
scenes.summary: At sunset Hermes takes fifty cattle from Pieria and reverses their tracks. He wears wicker sandals to hide his own, and bribes an old vine-tender at Onchestus to stay silent.
scenes.stakes: Hermes risks exposure and Apollo's anger if the theft is seen.

scenes.title: Fire at the Alpheus
scenes.summary: Hermes drives the cattle through the night to the Alpheus, feeds them in the byre, and makes fire with laurel sticks, the first fire-sticks.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet recalling Hermes' killing of the giant Argus.
Phoebus is a common epithet of Apollo.

notable_quotes.reason: Concisely sums up Hermes' precocious first day: born, lyre-player, cattle thief.
Gives the myth's origin of the tortoise-shell lyre.

analysis.text: The hymn celebrates Hermes' cunning intelligence, showing a newborn who outwits through invention and trickery.
The hymn explains the origins of the lyre, fire-making and sacrifice, and reflects Hermes' roles as patron of thieves, herdsmen and travellers.

legacy.text: Sophocles' satyr play Ichneutae (The Trackers) dramatised Hermes' theft of Apollo's cattle.

fun_facts.text: The text has a lacuna at line 41, so part of the fire-making passage is lost.

language_notes.text: Cyllene is a mountain in Arcadia, Hermes' birthplace; 'bare' is the archaic past tense of 'bear'.
'Of many shifts' means resourceful and full of tricks; 'blandly cunning' means smooth-talking and deceitful.
The fourth day of the month was sacred to Hermes in Greek tradition.
Meeting a tortoise is taken as an omen, a sign of coming fortune, as such signs were commonly read.
'Gaud' means a showy ornament; here it is the tortoise's patterned shell.
A living tortoise is said to guard against witchcraft; dead, its shell becomes the lyre's sounding body.
'Key' here probably means a plectrum, the tool for striking or plucking strings.
The 'taunts' simile compares his improvised singing to young men's playful, teasing verse exchanges at feasts.
"Steads" means places or farms where the cattle were kept; here, their accustomed pastures.
"Kine" is an archaic plural of "cow", meaning cattle.
"Straggling-wise" means in scattered, disordered fashion, so the herd's tracks look confused.
The cattle's hooves point the wrong way, and Hermes walks the opposite direction, so pursuers would read the trail backwards.
Tamarisk is a feathery-leaved shrub of sandy shores; myrtle is an evergreen shrub. Together they supply the pliant twigs for his sandals.
"Making shift" means improvising with what is at hand.
The final clause means: stay silent about matters that do not concern you, so no harm comes to you.
Selene is the Moon, here called daughter of Pallas, a Titan, son of Megamedes. Her "watch-post" is the sky's height.
Lotus here is a fodder plant, a clover-like grass, not the fruit of the Lotus-eaters.
The lacuna marks a gap in the manuscript; some lines describing the fire-drilling are lost.

context_notes.text: Hera is Zeus's wife, so the affair must be hidden from her; Zeus is called son of Cronos.
Apollo, called far-shooting for his bow, is the god whose cattle Hermes steals.
The seven strings match the standard early Greek lyre.
Pieria, north of Mount Olympus, is where Apollo's divine cattle graze. Hermes, newborn, is stealing from his elder half-brother.
"Slayer of Argus" refers to Hermes killing the hundred-eyed giant Argus, a common epithet of his.
Onchestus is a place in Boeotia, famed for a grove and shrine of Poseidon.
The Alpheus is a river in the Peloponnese, far south of Pieria, so the night drive covers a great distance.
The hymn credits Hermes with inventing fire-sticks, which are rubbed or twirled to produce fire. Laurel was Apollo's sacred tree.

literary_notes.text: A rapid list of titles defines Hermes as thief, trickster and night-prowler, foretelling the story.
Compressing birth, music and theft into a single day stresses his astonishing precocity.
Thought and flashing glances illustrate how instantly Hermes plans and acts together.
His hidden purpose, in contrast with the song, signals the coming cattle theft.
The reversed tracks show Hermes as a cunning trickster, already skilled at deception though newborn.
"Unthought of, unimagined" repeats the same idea in paired phrases, stressing the novelty of his invention.
Hermes offers a bribe with a veiled threat, asking the old man to ignore what he saw, which he will not do.
Night is a "dark ally" and the Moon climbs a watch-post, treating heavenly bodies as helpers and watchers.
